section_title: Order 1 Rule 1 — Who may be joined as plaintiffs
section_desc: All persons may be joined in one suit as plaintiffs in whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally or in the alternative, where if such persons brought separate suits, any common question of law or fact would arise.

section_title: Order 1 Rule 3 — Who may be joined as defendants
section_desc: All persons may be joined in one suit as defendants against whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally or in the alternative. Misjoinder and non-joinder of parties: No suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of parties.

section_title: Order 2 Rule 2 — Suit to include whole claim
section_desc: Every suit shall include the whole of the claim which the plaintiff is entitled to make in respect of the cause of action; but a plaintiff may relinquish any portion of his claim in order to bring the suit within the jurisdiction of any court. Rule of constructive res judicata — if plaintiff omits a part of his claim, he shall not afterwards sue in respect of the portion so omitted.

Every suit shall be instituted by presenting a plaint in duplicate to the Court or such officer as it appoints in this behalf. Every plaint shall comply with the rules contained in Orders VI and VII. A plaint shall not ordinarily be rejected on the ground of misjoinder unless the court decides to proceed with the suit. The plaint must be accompanied by an affidavit.

section_title: Order 5 Rule 1 — Issue and service of summons
section_desc: When a suit has been duly instituted, a summons may be issued to the defendant to appear and answer the claim and to file his written statement of defence. The summons shall be in the Form No. 1 in Appendix B. Court may also permit service through electronic transmission of documents including email or fax. The defendant must be given not less than thirty days to file his written statement after service of summons.

'Pleading' shall mean plaint or written statement. Every pleading shall contain and contain only a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim or defence, as the case may be, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved.

The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties. No application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has commenced, unless the Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before commencement of trial.

The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases: (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action; (b) where the relief claimed is undervalued; (c) where it is written on paper insufficiently stamped; (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law; (e) where it is not filed in duplicate; (f) where the plaintiff fails to comply with the provisions of Rule 9. Rejection of plaint is not a bar to fresh suit on same cause of action if not barred by limitation.

The defendant shall, within thirty days from the service of summons on him, present a written statement of his defence. Where the defendant fails to file the written statement within the said period, the Court shall pronounce judgment against him on the basis of the plaint unless the Court, for reasons to be recorded in writing, extends time not beyond ninety days from date of service of summons. After 2002 Amendment, thirty days is mandatory for filing written statement.

Where in a suit for recovery of money the defendant claims to set-off against the plaintiff's demand any ascertained sum of money legally recoverable by him from the plaintiff, and the amount claimed does not exceed the pecuniary limits of jurisdiction of the court, the defendant may, at the first hearing of the suit, but not afterwards unless permitted by the Court, present a written statement containing the particulars of the debt sought to be set-off.

section_title: Order 9 Rule 13 — Setting aside decree ex parte
section_desc: In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may apply to the Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, the Court shall make an order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit.
chapter_title: Appearance of Parties and Consequence of Non-Appearance

section_desc: Any party may, without filing any affidavit, apply to the Court for an order directing any other party to any suit to make discovery on oath of the documents which are or have been in his possession or power, relating to any matter in question in such suit. Discovery includes: interrogatories (written questions), inspection of documents, and admission of facts.

Where admissions of fact have been made either in the pleading or otherwise, whether orally or in writing, the Court may at any stage of the suit, either on the application of any party or of its own motion and without waiting for the determination of any other question between the parties, make such order or give such judgment as it may think fit, having regard to such admissions.

A plaintiff or a defendant may apply for a summary judgment in a suit at any time after summons has been served on defendant and before the Court has framed issues in the suit. The Court may give summary judgment without recording oral evidence where: the plaintiff has no real prospect of succeeding on a claim; or the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending a claim, and there is no other compelling reason why the claim or defence should not be disposed of before recording of oral evidence.

Issues arise when a material proposition of fact or law is affirmed by one party and denied by the other. Material propositions are those propositions of law or fact which a plaintiff must allege in order to show a right to sue or a defendant must allege in order to constitute his defence. Issues are of two kinds: issues of fact and issues of law. Courts shall frame and record issues at the first hearing before proceeding to trial.
chapter_title: Settlement of Issues and Determination of Suit on Issues of Law or on Issues Agreed Upon

section_desc: The Court shall hold a case management hearing, after the written statement has been filed and before framing of issues. At the case management hearing, the Court shall: consider whether alternative dispute resolution is appropriate; determine timeline for completion of pleadings; fix dates for examination of parties and witnesses; issue such further directions as may be necessary for expeditious disposal of the suit. Introduced by 2018 Amendment for commercial disputes.

section_title: Order 16 — Summoning and attendance of witnesses
section_desc: On or before such date as the Court may appoint, and not later than fifteen days after the date on which the issues are settled, the parties shall present in Court a list of witnesses whom they propose to call, either to give evidence or to produce documents, and obtain summonses to such persons for their attendance in Court. No witness shall be called to give evidence or to produce a document unless he is on the list of witnesses.

The Court may, if sufficient cause is shown, at any stage of the suit grant time to the parties or to any of them, and may from time to time adjourn the hearing of the suit. The Court shall not grant more than three adjournments to a party during the hearing of the suit. In granting adjournments, costs may be imposed on the party causing delay. The 2002 Amendment limits adjournments to prevent undue delay in civil litigation.

section_title: Order 18 Rule 2 — Statement and production of evidence
section_desc: On the day fixed for the hearing of the suit or on any other day to which the hearing is adjourned, the party having the right to begin shall state his case and produce his evidence in support of the issues which he is bound to prove. The other party shall then state his case and produce his evidence. The plaintiff generally has the right to begin. Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination shall follow the order prescribed.
chapter_title: Hearing of the Suit and Examination of Witnesses

section_desc: The Court, after the case has been heard, shall pronounce judgment in open Court, either at once, or as soon after as may be practicable and when the judgment is to be pronounced on some future day, the Court shall fix a day for that purpose of which due notice shall be given to the parties or their pleaders. Judgment shall state reasons for decision and findings on each issue.

section_title: Order 21 Rule 1 — Modes of paying money under decree
section_desc: Money payable under a decree may be paid: (a) into the Court whose duty it is to execute the decree; (b) out of Court to the decree-holder; (c) otherwise as the Court directs. All moneys shall, as far as possible, be paid within thirty days of the decree. Non-payment may attract execution proceedings.

section_title: Order 21 Rule 32 — Decree for specific performance
section_desc: Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has been made, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has wilfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced by his detention in civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both.

section_title: Order 21 Rule 54 — Attachment of immovable property
section_desc: Where the property to be attached is immovable, the attachment shall be made by an order prohibiting the judgment-debtor from transferring or charging the property in any way, and prohibiting all persons from taking any benefit under such transfer or charge. The attachment shall be announced by proclamation at some place on or adjacent to such property.

section_title: Order 21 Rule 64 — Sale of attached property
section_desc: Save as otherwise prescribed, where any property has been attached in execution of a decree, it shall be sold through public auction after due proclamation. The sale shall not be made before the end of fifteen days from the date of proclamation. The decree-holder or any person having a claim to or interest in the property may bid at the sale.

section_title: Order 22 — Death, marriage and insolvency of parties
section_desc: If a party to a suit dies and the right to sue survives, the suit shall not abate on the death of such party, if the right to sue survives. Where one of two or more plaintiffs or defendants dies and the right to sue survives to the surviving plaintiff or against the surviving defendant, the Court shall cause the death to be recorded, and the suit shall proceed.
chapter_title: Death, Marriage and Insolvency of Parties

section_desc: At any time after the institution of a suit, the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, abandon his suit or abandon a part of his claim: The Court may, on such terms as it thinks fit, allow the plaintiff to withdraw from a suit or to abandon part of a claim, with liberty to file a fresh suit for the subject matter of the suit or abandoned part if the plaintiff satisfies the Court that there are sufficient grounds for doing so.

Any Court may in any suit issue a commission: to examine any person; to make a local investigation; to examine or adjust accounts; to make a partition; for the holding of a scientific, technical, or expert investigation; for the sale of movable property; for performing any ministerial act. A commission to examine a witness may be issued when the witness is exempted from appearing in Court, is unable to attend Court from sickness or infirmity, or resides outside the local limits of jurisdiction.

section_title: Order 32 — Suits by or against minors and persons of unsound mind
section_desc: Every suit by a minor shall be instituted in his name by a person who in such suit shall be called the next friend of the minor. A minor may be appointed guardian ad litem for a suit. No next friend or guardian for the suit shall, without leave of the Court: receive any movable property on behalf of the minor; or give any receipt for the recovery of any immovable property.
chapter_title: Suits by or Against Minors and Persons of Unsound Mind

section_title: Order 33 — Suits by indigent persons (Pauper suits)
section_desc: Any suit may be instituted by an indigent person. A person is an indigent person if he is not possessed of sufficient means (other than property exempt from attachment in execution of a decree and the subject-matter of the suit) to enable him to pay the fee prescribed for the plaint; or where no such fee is prescribed, if he is not entitled to property worth one thousand rupees. On admission, the plaintiff is exempted from court fees.

section_title: Order 34 — Suits relating to mortgages of immoveable property
section_desc: In a suit for foreclosure of the mortgage of immoveable property, the Court shall pass a preliminary decree in which the mortgage money due shall be ascertained and the mortgagor shall be directed to pay into Court by a certain date the amount so found due. If the mortgagor fails to pay within the period allowed, the Court shall pass a final decree debarring the mortgagor from all right to redeem the property. The decree shall specify the relief granted — sale or foreclosure.
chapter_title: Suits Relating to Mortgages of Immoveable Property

section_desc: The following suits may be instituted as summary suits: suits upon bills of exchange, hundis or promissory notes; suits in which plaintiff seeks to recover a debt or liquidated demand in money payable by the defendant with or without interest, arising on a written contract, or on an enactment, or on a guarantee (where the claim against the principal is in respect of a debt or liquidated demand), for a sum not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Leave to defend must be obtained by defendant.

Where at any stage of a suit, the Court is satisfied, by affidavit or otherwise, that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree that may be passed against him, is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property, or is about to remove the whole or any part of his property from the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, the Court may direct the defendant to furnish security, in such sum as may be specified in the order, to produce and place at the disposal of the Court, when directed, such property or the value of the same.

section_title: Order 39 Rule 1 — Temporary injunction when granted
section_desc: Where in any suit it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit, or wrongfully sold in execution of a decree, or that the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to defraud his creditors, the Court may by order grant a temporary injunction to restrain such act, or make such other order for the purpose of staying and preventing the wasting, damaging, alienation, sale, removal or disposition of the property as the Court thinks fit.

Every appeal from a decree shall be made by a memorandum signed by the appellant or his pleader, and presented to the Appellate Court or to such officer as it appoints in this behalf. The memorandum shall contain: the grounds of objection to the decree appealed from; the decision or finding objected to. The court fee must accompany the memo of appeal. The appeal should be filed within the prescribed limitation period — generally 30-90 days.

An appeal shall lie from the following orders: order refusing to set aside proceeding for non-appearance; order deciding a question relating to jurisdiction; order granting or refusing a temporary injunction; order granting or refusing an attachment before judgment; order deciding a question relating to arbitration; order appointing or refusing to appoint a commissioner; order setting aside or refusing to set aside an ex parte decree.

Any person considering himself aggrieved by a decree or order may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order on the following grounds: discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed; on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record; or for any other sufficient reason.

section_title: Section 151 — Saving of inherent powers of Court
section_desc: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. The inherent powers under Section 151 CPC are residual and cannot be used to circumvent express provisions. They are used to fill lacunae in procedural law when justice so requires.

section_title: Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property
section_desc: If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he claims may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. No suit under this section shall be brought after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession. No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section.

section_title: Specific performance of part of contract
section_desc: Except as provided in this Chapter, the Court shall not direct the specific performance of a part of a contract. The Court may direct specific performance of a part of a contract where: a part of a contract is incapable of being performed specifically; a party has performed his part and the remainder is capable of specific performance; where the defect in the right of the party unable to perform is not one that affects the main subject of the contract.

section_title: Relief against parties and persons claiming under them by subsequent title
section_desc: Except as otherwise provided by this Chapter, specific performance of a contract may be enforced against: either party thereto; any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract.

Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of section 10, the party who suffers from a breach of contract may get the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency, and recover expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered by him, from the party committing such breach. The party is entitled to recover the actual cost of substituted performance; he cannot claim excess over market rate. Notice must be given to the defaulting party before substituted performance.

When, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing does not express their real intention, then either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; and, if the Court find that the alleged fraud or mistake is proved and that the instrument if rectified would be such as the parties would have been bound to perform, it may, in its discretion direct rectification of the instrument.

Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled. A deed obtained by fraud or coercion may be cancelled by court order.

An injunction cannot be granted to restrain any person from prosecuting a judicial proceeding pending at the institution of the suit in which the injunction is asked; to restrain any person from instituting or prosecuting any proceeding in a court not subordinate to that from which injunction is sought; to restrain any person from applying to any legislative body; to restrain any person from instituting or prosecuting any proceeding in a criminal matter.

In this Act: 'applicant' includes a petitioner; 'application' includes a petition; 'defendant' includes all persons served with summons or notice of an application; 'period of limitation' means the period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by the Schedule, and 'prescribed period' means the period of limitation computed in accordance with the provisions of this Act; 'suit' does not include an appeal or an application; 'tort' means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Where a person entitled to institute a suit or make an application for the execution of a decree is, at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned, a minor, or insane, or an idiot, he may institute the suit or make the application within the same period after the disability has ceased, as would otherwise have been allowed from the time specified therefor in the third column of the Schedule.

section_title: Disability of one of several persons
section_desc: Where one of several persons jointly entitled to institute a suit or make an application for the execution of a decree is under any such disability, and a discharge can be given without the concurrence of such person, time will run against them all; but, where no such discharge can be given, time will not run as against any of them until one of them becomes capable of giving such discharge without the concurrence of others or until the disability has ceased.

Nothing in sections 4 to 7 shall apply to suits to enforce rights of pre-emption; and in cases where a suit has been instituted on behalf of or against a minor or other person under disability to show that he had the same or better right as the plaintiff or defendant in the pending suit.

section_title: Suits against trustees and their representatives
section_desc: Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing provisions of this Act, no suit by a beneficiary against a trustee or his representative to recover trust property or in respect of any breach of trust, not being a suit to which any of the following sections applies, shall be barred by any length of time.

section_title: Suits on contracts entered into outside India
section_desc: The period of limitation shall be the same as it would be in India for a suit for the same cause of action. The period of limitation shall not be governed by the law of the place where the contract was made; it shall be governed by Indian limitation law.

No suit shall be brought after the expiry of the period prescribed for the suit; yet the period of limitation shall not apply to suits for declaration of title to immovable property where the plaintiff is and has been in possession for a period of twelve years before filing the suit — Adverse Possession. The person in adverse possession for twelve years acquires a right to sue.

At the determination of the period hereby limited to any person for instituting a suit for possession of any property, his right to such property shall be extinguished. This applies specifically to suits for recovery of immovable property — after expiry of limitation, the plaintiff's right to sue as well as his title itself gets extinguished.

section_title: Schedule Article 1 — Suit on account stated
section_desc: Period of limitation: 3 years. Time from which period begins to run: when the account is stated. Application: Suits for recovery of money on an account stated between parties — where both parties have agreed on the balance due.

Period of limitation: 3 years. Time from which period begins to run: when the right to sue first accrues. Application: Suits for declaratory relief where plaintiff seeks a declaration of his legal status or right to property. The period runs from when the right to declaration first arises.

section_title: Schedule Article 65 — Suit for possession of immovable property or hereditary office
section_desc: Period of limitation: 12 years. Time from which period begins to run: when the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff. Application: The most important article for property disputes — suits for possession of immovable property. If adverse possession continues for 12 years, title is extinguished.

section_title: Schedule Article 113 — Suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere
section_desc: Period of limitation: 3 years. Time from which period begins to run: when the right to sue accrues. Application: Residuary article — applies to all suits not covered by any other article in the Schedule. Most contract suits fall here. Important for civil litigation as the default limitation period.

In this Act: 'book' includes a portion of a book and also any number of sheets connected together; 'district' means a district for the purposes of this Act, as constituted under section 6 of this Act; 'immovable property' includes land, buildings, hereditary allowances, rights to ways, lights, ferries, fisheries or any other benefit to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth; 'lease' means a lease of immovable property; 'minor' means a person who has not completed eighteen years of age; 'movable property' means property of every description, except immovable property; 'registered' means registered in accordance with the provisions of this Act applicable to the document presented for registration.

section_title: Documents of which registration is optional
section_desc: The following documents may be registered under this Act: instruments (other than instruments of gift) relating to the lease of immovable property for any term not exceeding one year, and instruments of lease exempted under section 17; instruments transferring or assigning any decree or order of a court or any award; documents relating to movable property.

Subject to the provisions contained in sections 24, 25 and 26, no document other than a will shall be accepted for registration unless presented for that purpose to the proper officer within four months from the date of its execution. Where a document is executed by several persons at different times, it may be presented for registration within four months from the date of each execution.

section_title: Persons who may present documents for registration
section_desc: Except in the cases mentioned in sections 31, 88 and 89, every document to be registered under this Act shall be presented at the proper registration office by some person executing or claiming under the document or his representative, assign or agent duly authorized by a power of attorney executed and authenticated in the manner hereinafter mentioned.
chapter_title: Persons Who May Present Documents for Registration

section_title: Effect of non-registration of documents required to be registered
section_desc: No document required by section 17 or by any provision of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, to be registered shall: affect any immovable property comprised therein; confer any power to adopt; be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property or conferring such power, unless it has been registered. A document which fails to be registered for want of stamp cannot be registered.

After a document has been duly registered under this Act, the registering officer shall endorse thereon a certificate containing the word 'Registered,' together with the number and page of the book in which the document has been copied. Such certificate shall be signed, sealed and dated by the registering officer. Documents shall be returned after such endorsement.

In this Act: 'executed' and 'execution', used with reference to instruments, mean signed and signature; 'impressed stamp' means a stamp impressed by means of a die; 'instrument' includes every document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished or recorded; 'stamped' and 'duly stamped' describe an instrument on which an impressed or adhesive stamp of not less than the proper amount has been affixed; 'value' in section 20 means the amount for which the instrument is executed or the consideration expressed.

section_title: Instruments executed in India — Time for stamping
section_desc: All instruments chargeable with duty and executed by any person in India shall be stamped before or at the time of execution. An instrument not so stamped is not void — it is merely not receivable in evidence unless the duty and penalty are paid. The distinction between registration and stamping must be noted — an instrument may be registered but still inadmissible if unstamped.

section_title: Facts affecting duty to be set forth in instrument
section_desc: The consideration (if any) and all other facts and circumstances affecting the chargeability of any instrument with duty, or the amount of the duty with which it is chargeable, shall be fully and truly set forth therein. Non-disclosure or understatement of consideration leads to evasion of stamp duty and is punishable.

When any instrument, whether executed or not and whether previously stamped or not, is brought to a Collector, and the person bringing it applies to have the opinion of that officer as to the duty (if any) with which it is chargeable, and pays a fee of such amount (not exceeding five rupees and not less than fifty naye paise), the Collector shall determine the duty, if any, with which, in his judgment, the instrument is chargeable.

Every person having by law or consent of parties authority to receive evidence, and every person in charge of a public office, before whom any instrument, chargeable, in his opinion, with duty, is produced or comes in the performance of his functions, shall, if it appears to him that such instrument is not duly stamped, impound the same. An impounded document may be admitted in evidence on payment of duty and penalty.

section_title: Admission of instrument in evidence on payment of duty and penalty
section_desc: When an instrument has been impounded, the impounding officer may, on payment of the duty with which the instrument is chargeable, together with a penalty of five times the amount of the proper duty or deficient portion thereof, admit the instrument in evidence. No instrument shall be admitted in evidence which has been impounded unless and until the duty and penalty are paid.

If the registering officer, while registering any instrument transferring any property, has reason to believe that the true market value of such property has not been set forth in the instrument, he may after registering such instrument, refer the same to the Collector for determination of the true market value of such property and the proper duty payable thereon. This section inserted to prevent undervaluation of property to evade stamp duty.
